The first jobs AI is cutting may not be at headquarters. They may be in somebody else's office, in another country.

On 23 November Anthropic published "Working with AI", based on 66 interviews at 58 of its US enterprise customers. The headline is reassuring: very few AI-driven layoffs. Read further and it is less comfortable.

By the numbers
- 2 of 58: companies where AI automation fully eliminated a position and someone lost their job.
- Two-thirds: companies reporting reduced hiring due to AI. "We may not be firing, but we're not hiring."
- 9: companies that cut contracted developers, customer service, legal or back-office work, much of it already offshored.
- Well over 100: offshore data and developer contractors one finance company let go.
- More than 90%: the cut in planned reviewer hiring at one firm after an AI document-review agent.

Caveats: these are Anthropic's own customers, not a representative sample, and Anthropic frames the contractor cuts as a possible early warning, not a proven trend.

Why the outsourced work goes first
Offshore work tends to be modular: self-contained tasks that can be handed off, sometimes with modest quality expectations. That is exactly what an AI agent can now take over. One executive said of an offshore design firm: "We've since fired them."

Cutting a vendor contract does not show up as a layoff in anyone's headcount data. That is why the domestic numbers look calm.

The regional read
The Philippines is the obvious exposure. IBPAP projects IT-BPM revenue of US$42.3bn and 1.94 million full-time staff in 2026, rising to US$45bn and 1.99 million in 2027. Revenue growth of 6.4% against headcount growth of 2.6%. Revenue per worker edges from about US$21,800 to US$22,600 (42.3 / 1.94 versus 45 / 1.99).

IBPAP's chief said it may mean fewer employees. My read: the industry is already pricing it in.

What this means for us
Many Singapore SMEs outsource exactly this kind of work: bookkeeping, data entry, first-line customer service, design production. Three questions worth asking this quarter:
- Which outsourced tasks are modular enough for an agent to take over, and what would it cost to try?
- If you are a vendor, which of your services are a handoff and which are judgement your client cannot replicate?
- Who in-house would review the agent's output? Anthropic's interviewees found the review work does not disappear.

Leadership Takeaway: the quietest AI job impact is the contract you do not renew. Plan for it from both sides of the table.

If you outsource today, would you replace the vendor, or ask the vendor to bring the AI?

You need someone who has designed a fault-tolerant event stream that ingests real-time risk signals, who understands how to validate data integrity before it reaches an autonomous agent, and who can build the execution layer that turns a passive control tower into an active, self-correcting supply chain. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these systems-thinking principles to help a team move from reactive visibility to proactive, signal-driven resilience.

Make or buy used to have a seat in every operations discussion. For software, the answer went quiet a long time ago: buy.

Most of that still holds. Nobody is cancelling an SAP licence because AI coding tools exist. My question is about everything else.

Buying software for a small job costs far more than the licence. There is the vendor search, the demos, procurement, the security review, the contract and the integration project. For a small job, that overhead is bigger than the job, so the job never gets done. Now one or two people with AI tools can build a small, specific piece of software in days. When making costs less than the paperwork of buying, the decision reopens. It reopens at the edge of the business, not at the core.

Here is an invented example. A 140-person stamping plant in Ontario gets a January gas bill 30 percent higher than the year before. The heating contractor finds nothing wrong. The plant engineer suspects the shipping doors, but the evidence sits in four systems that have never met: the door sensors, the forklift tracking, the rooftop heating units and the shipping appointments in the ERP. Each answers questions about itself. None can say why door 4 is open.

No vendor sells that answer, and none ever will. It is a question about one dock at one plant.

So she makes it. She is not a programmer. In a week of afternoons with an AI assistant, she builds a small program that puts the four records on one clock. Door 4 turns out to be open three hours a day for less than one hour of loading, because one carrier arrives late and the crew opens the door at the appointment time. The fix is a radio call from the gatehouse, not software.

That is discretionary work. It only reads data the equipment already produces. If it stopped tomorrow, the plant would still run.

I would be careful, though. We have been here before: spreadsheets and departmental databases each left behind tools nobody owned once their author moved on. Writing software was never the expensive part. Owning it for ten years was. And when the supervisor asks whether the program can just close the door, the right answer is no. Reading a door's history is one thing. Moving a dock door is a safety system.

So is in-house development about to have a renaissance? At the core of the business, I doubt it. Around the edge, in the work that connects systems and uses data nobody had time to use, I think it may already have started.

If companies make more, who sells less? And does hiring on the buyers' side make up for it? Those are the next two posts. I would like to hear what you are seeing.

A Marxist view of the economy says that value can only be generated by human work. Even when you automate something, you are just shifting the value generation somewhere else.

I decided to test this against the "AI layoffs" of the last few years. What actually happened to those companies?

Turns out, the human work didn't vanish. It just moved around, and many of the biggest posters for AI cuts ended up with MORE employees than before:

• SAP announced a €3B "AI-first" restructuring affecting ~10,000 roles in 2024. Yet total headcount grew from 107,602 (2023) to over 113,000 by late 2026.
• Duolingo cut 10% of contract translators for AI, then grew full-time staff nearly 50% (720 to ~1,075) to build and validate those pipelines.
• Amazon cut ~30,000 corporate roles citing AI, yet total global headcount rose from 1.52M to 1.63M+ as logistics, warehouse, and data center teams expanded.

Even when companies actually tried to shrink, they hit a wall:

• Klarna cut its workforce nearly in half and bragged AI did the work of 700 agents. By 2025/2026, the CEO admitted they went too far as quality tanked, and they started rehiring humans.
• IBM froze junior hiring for AI in 2023, only to reverse course in 2026 and triple entry-level hiring to supervise AI pipelines.

Industry data backs this up: over half of executives who did AI-driven layoffs later regretted it, and roughly 1 in 3 companies ended up reopening the exact roles they cut, often paying a premium to bring people back.

And the companies that actually did shrink internal headcount? They didn't delete the labor. They just moved it onto their CapEx balance sheet, paying Nvidia, TSMC, power utilities, and data center construction crews instead of salaried staff.

Automation doesn't erase human work. It just moves the bill.

Three technical, client-facing roles. Three different jobs. Hiring the wrong one is a quiet way for an AI project to stall. 🧩

🛠️ Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE): embeds with you to build and ship production AI in your own environment, on your data. Accountable for a production outcome, not a document.
🤝 Solutions engineer: usually works for a software vendor. Helps you see the product work on your problem and get it configured well enough to adopt. Very useful once you've chosen a platform.
📋 Consultant: advises on direction. Many engagements end at the recommendation.

A quick test: if the work is a regulated workflow that must run in your environment, with controls no off-the-shelf product provides, it isn't a configuration task. It's an implementation, and that's FDE work.

One more line worth drawing: an FDE isn't staff augmentation either. Adding a contractor for a number of hours with no outcome attached is a different contract.

Less hiring at certain orgs, holidays impact market, less jobs.

What you do now determines your 2027.

Every holiday season, Tech jobseekers feel pinched.
→ More hiring teams offline for holidays
→ Some tech companies freeze full-time hiring
→ Some orgs are just focused on the year’s priorities
→ Throw the hairy mess AI has made of the market, as a fun lil’ bonus

And w/all this stuff, your inbox looks emptier than usual..and you panic.

So, you follow up w/your network yet AGAIN, but only get crickets & tumbleweeds. 
Play budget bingo w/your unemployment to get gifts for the kids.
Apply for the scant roles available, even if beneath you.
By Dec, you’re in survival mode..and praying Jan brings a job.

It doesn’t gotta be that way.

Here’s the truth:

The holiday season doesn’t kill job offers.
A perceived slow season doesn’t keep you unemployed.
Poor prep combined with the wrong attitude does.
But with good prep & the right attitude, you'll get traction even in supposedly slow months.

Take my job hunts, for example.

I used such an effective strategy that even w/the drop in hiring in Oct-Dec, I've landed multiple FAANG & FAANG-coded roles in autumns/winters.

Here's how:

 1️⃣ - I actively decoded the hiring slowdown - then exploited it

Asked myself questions like these:
(and effing acted on them)

- What target orgs historically tend to increase FT hiring for my target role title during the holidays?
- What additional companies are forecasted to increase or keep hiring?
(knowing why is key for strategy too ^_^)
- Which companies/teams have “use it or lose it” annual talent budget?
- Which companies will need help not only on seasonal campaigns/projects, but also come the new year?
- Any seasonal contracts w/full-time conversion potential? Or at least opportunity to make money and be a bridge to my next FT role?
- How much is there actually a holiday slowdown..and how much am I giving in to stuff like overblown social media noise?

 2️⃣ - I went all-in on external networking 

Targeted companies w/immediate yet long-term needs hiring for positions I wanted, and charmed the crap outta their hiring teams, sometimes before even getting in an interview room. 
You'd be surprised how many folks actually work during the holidays - and you'll be a stand-out candidate if you keep engaging w/them thoughtfully.

3️⃣ - I stayed consistent while others got sucked into the holiday hole

While others got schnackered at home off spiked egg nog and watched bad Hallmark movies past midnight, I did the same.
But also stayed consistent w/my job search system. 

-

It's not easy, but it's simple:

→ Still enjoy your fave holidays
→ Go all in on networking
→ Stay in motion
→ Keep convos going
→ Don't fall for "holiday hiring slowdown" hype
→ Healthily hustle while others tussle w/competing holiday commitments

→ Set yourself up for a killer 2027  💯
